stem: Define growth, differentiation, development, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, determinate growth, meristem and growth rate.
solution:
1. **Growth**: an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ or its parts or even of an individual cell. It is generally accompanied by metabolic processes (both anabolic and catabolic) that occur at the expense of energy.
2. **Differentiation**: the act leading to maturation, in which cells derived from the root apical and shoot apical meristems and cambium undergo structural changes in their cell walls and protoplasm to perform specific functions.
3. **Development**: all the changes that an organism goes through during its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence. It is the sum of growth and differentiation.
4. **Dedifferentiation**: the phenomenon in which living differentiated cells, which had lost the capacity to divide, regain the capacity of division under certain conditions, e.g., formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells.
5. **Redifferentiation**: the process in which cells produced by dedifferentiated tissues once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions.
6. **Determinate growth**: growth that stops once the organ reaches a certain size, so the organ has limited dimensions, e.g., leaves, flowers and fruits.
7. **Meristem**: a group of cells at certain locations in the plant body that have the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate, e.g., root apical meristem, shoot apical meristem and vascular cambium.
8. **Growth rate**: the increased growth per unit time.
groundedIn: §13.1; §13.2; §13.3; §13.1.1; §13.1.4; §13.0 — growth as irreversible permanent increase with metabolism; differentiation, dedifferentiation (interfascicular and cork cambium from parenchyma), redifferentiation; development from germination to senescence, sum of growth and differentiation; meristem cells divide and self-perpetuate; growth rate as increased growth per unit time; leaves, flowers and fruits have limited dimensions; BEYOND CHAPTER: the definition of determinate growth as growth that stops once a certain size is reached

stem: Why is not any one parameter good enough to demonstrate growth throughout the life of a flowering plant?
solution:
No single parameter can follow growth through the whole life of a flowering plant, because growth is expressed differently in different organs and at different stages.

1. Growth at the cellular level is an increase in the amount of **protoplasm**, which is difficult to measure directly. So a quantity roughly **proportional** to it is measured: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume or cell number.
2. Different organs grow in different ways. A **maize root apical meristem** grows by increase in **cell number** (more than 17,500 new cells per hour); **watermelon** cells grow by increase in **cell size** (up to 3,50,000 times); a **pollen tube** grows in **length**; a **dorsiventral leaf** grows in **surface area**.
3. The plant passes through different phases: the meristematic phase (cell division), the elongation phase (cell enlargement) and the maturation phase (wall thickening). Later, **secondary growth** increases the **girth** of organs rather than their length.
4. Hence a parameter suited to one organ or one phase (e.g., length) misses growth that appears as weight, area, cell number or girth elsewhere, and several parameters must be used together.
groundedIn: §13.1.2; §13.1.3; §13.1.1 — growth as increase in protoplasm, measured indirectly by fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number; maize root apex, watermelon, pollen tube, dorsiventral leaf; meristematic, elongation and maturation phases; lateral meristems increase girth in secondary growth

solution:
In **arithmetic growth**, following mitotic cell division, **only one daughter cell continues to divide** while the other differentiates and matures.

1. The simplest example is a **root elongating at a constant rate**.
2. A plot of the length of the organ against time gives a **linear curve** (Fig. 13.5).
3. It is expressed as \(L_t = L_0 + rt\), where \(L_t\) is the length at time t, \(L_0\) is the length at time zero and r is the growth rate (elongation per unit time).
groundedIn: §13.1.4; Fig. 13.4; Fig. 13.5 — only one daughter cell continues to divide; root elongating at a constant rate; linear curve; Lt = L0 + rt

solution:
In **geometric growth**, following mitotic cell division, **both progeny cells retain the ability to divide** and continue to do so.

1. The initial growth is slow (**lag phase**); it then increases rapidly at an exponential rate (**log or exponential phase**).
2. With limited nutrient supply the growth slows down, leading to a **stationary phase**; the plot of growth against time is a sigmoid curve.
3. Exponential growth is expressed as \(W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}\), where \(W_1\) is the final size (weight, height, number etc.), \(W_0\) the initial size, r the growth rate, t the time of growth and e the base of natural logarithms.
4. Here r is the **relative growth rate**, a measure of the ability of the plant to produce new plant material, called the **efficiency index**. So the final size \(W_1\) depends on the initial size \(W_0\).
groundedIn: §13.1.4; Fig. 13.4 — both progeny cells retain the ability to divide; lag, log and stationary phases; W1 = W0 e^rt; r as relative growth rate and efficiency index

solution:
A **sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve** is obtained when a parameter of growth is plotted against time for a living system showing geometric growth.

1. **Lag phase**: the initial growth is slow.
2. **Log (exponential) phase**: growth increases rapidly at an exponential rate, as both progeny cells of each division keep dividing.
3. **Stationary phase**: with limited nutrient supply, growth slows down and levels off.

The sigmoid curve is characteristic of living organisms growing in a natural environment. It is typical of all cells, tissues and organs of a plant, and of cells in culture (Fig. 13.6).
groundedIn: §13.1.4; Fig. 13.6 — lag, exponential and stationary phases give a typical sigmoid or S-curve, characteristic of organisms in a natural environment and typical of all cells, tissues and organs of a plant

solution:
**Absolute growth rate** is the measurement and comparison of **total growth per unit time**. **Relative growth rate** is the growth of the given system per unit time **expressed on a common basis**, e.g., per unit initial parameter.

| Basis | Absolute growth rate | Relative growth rate |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Total growth per unit time | Growth per unit time per unit initial parameter |
| Initial size | Not taken into account | Taken into account |
| Leaves A and B (Fig. 13.7) | Equal: both increase in area by \(5\ \text{cm}^2\) in the given time | Much higher in the smaller leaf A (\(5 \to 10\ \text{cm}^2\), doubled) than in leaf B (\(50 \to 55\ \text{cm}^2\), a one-tenth increase) |
groundedIn: §13.1.4; Fig. 13.7 — absolute growth rate as total growth per unit time; relative growth rate per unit initial parameter; leaves A (5 to 10 cm2) and B (50 to 55 cm2) both increase by 5 cm2

stem: List five main groups of natural plant growth regulators. Write a note on discovery, physiological functions and agricultural/horticultural applications of any one of them.
solution:
**Five main groups of natural plant growth regulators:** (1) **auxins**, (2) **gibberellins**, (3) **cytokinins**, (4) **abscisic acid** and (5) **ethylene**.

**Note on auxins**

**Discovery**
1. Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin observed that the **coleoptiles of canary grass** grew towards a unilateral light source (**phototropism**). Experiments showed that the **tip of the coleoptile** was the site of a transmittable influence that caused the bending of the entire coleoptile.
2. **F.W. Went** isolated auxin from the **tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings**.
3. Auxin (Greek 'auxein': to grow) was first isolated from human urine. **IAA** and **IBA** have been isolated from plants; **NAA** and **2, 4-D** are synthetic auxins.

**Physiological functions**
1. Auxins are produced by the growing apices of stems and roots, from where they migrate to the regions of their action.
2. They cause **apical dominance**: the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds.
3. They prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote the **abscission** of older mature leaves and fruits.
4. They control **xylem differentiation** and help in cell division.

**Agricultural/horticultural applications**
1. Initiate **rooting in stem cuttings**, widely used for plant propagation.
2. Promote **flowering**, e.g., in pineapples.
3. Induce **parthenocarpy**, e.g., in tomatoes.
4. Used as **herbicides**: 2, 4-D kills dicotyledonous weeds but does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants, so gardeners use it to prepare weed-free lawns.
5. **Decapitation** (removal of shoot tips) removes apical dominance and makes the lateral buds grow, as applied in tea plantations and hedge-making.
groundedIn: §13.4.2; §13.4.3.1; Fig. 13.10; Fig. 13.11 — five major groups of PGRs (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene; stated in the chapter Summary); Darwins' canary grass coleoptiles, Went's oat coleoptile tips; auxin from human urine; IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D; apical dominance, abscission, xylem differentiation; rooting, flowering in pineapple, parthenocarpy in tomato, herbicide, tea plantations and hedge-making

stem: Why is abscisic acid also known as stress hormone?
solution:
Abscisic acid (ABA) is called the **stress hormone** because it **increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of stresses**.

1. ABA stimulates the **closure of stomata**, which reduces water loss when water is scarce.
2. It plays an important role in plant responses to **wounds and stresses of biotic and abiotic origin**.
3. By inducing **dormancy**, ABA helps seeds to withstand **desiccation** and other factors unfavourable for growth.
4. It acts as a general **plant growth inhibitor** and an inhibitor of plant metabolism, and it inhibits seed germination, so growth is held back under unfavourable conditions.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.5; §13.4.1 — ABA stimulates closure of stomata and increases tolerance to various kinds of stresses, hence called the stress hormone; inducing dormancy helps seeds withstand desiccation; general growth inhibitor; PGRs of this group respond to wounds and biotic and abiotic stresses

stem: 'Both growth and differentiation in higher plants are open'. Comment.
solution:
Both growth and differentiation in higher plants are **open**, i.e., not fixed or limited in advance.

**Growth is open**
1. Plants retain the capacity for **unlimited growth** throughout their life because of **meristems** at certain locations in the body, whose cells have the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate.
2. New cells are always being added to the plant body by the activity of the meristem; this is the **open form of growth**. Root and shoot apical meristems cause primary growth (elongation), and the lateral meristems, vascular cambium and cork cambium, cause secondary growth (girth).

**Differentiation is open**
1. Cells/tissues arising out of the **same meristem** have **different structures at maturity**.
2. The final structure of a cell or tissue is also determined by its **location**: cells positioned away from the root apical meristem differentiate as **root-cap cells**, while those pushed to the periphery mature as **epidermis**.
3. Differentiated cells can also **dedifferentiate** (e.g., parenchyma forming interfascicular cambium and cork cambium) and then **redifferentiate**.

Since differentiation is open, development in plants is flexible too, and plants show **plasticity**, e.g., heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur and buttercup.
groundedIn: §13.1.1; §13.2; §13.3; Fig. 13.9 — meristems give unlimited, open form of growth; primary and secondary growth; cells from the same meristem have different structures at maturity; root-cap and epidermis by position; dedifferentiation and redifferentiation; plasticity and heterophylly

stem: 'Both a short day plant and a long day plant can produce can flower simultaneously in a given place'. Explain.
solution:
Both can flower together because each plant flowers according to whether the day length is above or below **its own critical photoperiod**, not according to a single fixed day length. (The book's 'can produce can flower' is a misprint for 'can flower'.)

1. Light is an extrinsic factor that controls the initiation of **flowering**. The response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night is called **photoperiodism**.
2. A **short day plant (SDP)** flowers when the day length is **shorter than its critical photoperiod**.
3. A **long day plant (LDP)** flowers when the day length is **longer than its critical photoperiod**.
4. The critical photoperiod differs from species to species. If, for example, an SDP has a critical photoperiod of 14 hours and an LDP one of 12 hours, a 13-hour day is shorter than the SDP's critical length and longer than the LDP's.
5. Both plants then receive their inductive photoperiod at the same time, so they flower **simultaneously** in that place.
groundedIn: §13.4.3; §13.3 — extrinsic factors such as light control development and flowering via PGR; BEYOND CHAPTER: photoperiodism; an SDP flowers below and an LDP above its own critical photoperiod; the critical photoperiod differs between species (the 14 h and 12 h values are an illustration, not data)

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
solution: **Auxin**, e.g., **IBA** or **NAA**. Auxins help to initiate rooting in stem cuttings, an application widely used for plant propagation.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.1 — auxins help to initiate rooting in stem cuttings; IBA and NAA as auxins

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
solution: **Ethylene**, usually applied as **ethephon**, which releases ethylene slowly in the plant. Ethylene is highly effective in fruit ripening and enhances the respiration rate during ripening; ethephon hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.4 — ethylene is highly effective in fruit ripening and enhances respiration during ripening; ethephon releases ethylene slowly and hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
solution: **Cytokinin**. Cytokinins promote **nutrient mobilisation**, which helps in the delay of leaf senescence.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.3 — cytokinins promote nutrient mobilisation which helps in the delay of leaf senescence

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
solution: **Cytokinin**. Cytokinins help overcome **apical dominance** and promote **lateral shoot growth**, so the axillary buds grow into branches.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.3 — cytokinins help to produce lateral shoot growth and help overcome the apical dominance

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
solution: **Gibberellin** (e.g., \(\text{GA}_3\)). Gibberellins promote **bolting**, i.e., internode elongation just prior to flowering, in beet, cabbages and many plants with rosette habit.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.2 — gibberellins promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering) in beet, cabbages and plants with rosette habit

context: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to:
stem: induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves.
solution: **Abscisic acid (ABA)**. ABA stimulates the **closure of stomata** and increases the tolerance of plants to stress.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.5 — ABA stimulates the closure of stomata and increases tolerance to stresses

stem: Would a defoliated plant respond to photoperiodic cycle? Why?
solution:
**No.** A defoliated plant would not respond to a photoperiodic cycle, because the **leaves** are the site where the light and dark periods are **perceived**.

1. Light is an extrinsic factor that controls the initiation of flowering through plant growth regulators.
2. The photoperiod is perceived by the **leaves**, which then produce a hormonal flowering stimulus that moves to the **shoot apices**.
3. Only after receiving this stimulus are the shoot apices modified into flowering apices.
4. A defoliated plant has no leaves to perceive the photoperiod, so no stimulus reaches the shoot apex and the plant does not flower in response to the photoperiodic cycle.
groundedIn: §13.4.3; §13.3 — extrinsic factors such as light control flowering via PGR; BEYOND CHAPTER: the leaves perceive the photoperiod; a hormonal flowering stimulus moves from the leaves to the shoot apices, which then become flowering apices

context: What would be expected to happen if:
solution:
The rice seedlings would show the symptoms of the **'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease**: they would grow **abnormally tall** through excessive elongation of the stem.

1. Bakanae is caused by the fungal pathogen Gibberella fujikuroi. E. Kurosawa (1926) produced its symptoms in rice seedlings by treating them with sterile filtrates of the fungus.
2. The active substance in the filtrate was later identified as **gibberellic acid**.
3. Gibberellins cause an **increase in length of axis** (internode elongation), so applying \(\text{GA}_3\) directly reproduces the disease symptoms.
groundedIn: §13.4.2; §13.4.3.2 — bakanae caused by Gibberella fujikuroi; Kurosawa's sterile filtrates; active substance gibberellic acid; GAs increase the length of axis; BEYOND CHAPTER: the bakanae symptom is abnormal, excessive elongation of the rice seedlings

context: What would be expected to happen if:
solution:
The cells would go on dividing without maturing, forming a **mass of undifferentiated cells** like a **callus**; no specialised tissues or organs would form.

1. **Differentiation** is the act leading to maturation, by which cells derived from meristems undergo structural changes to perform **specific functions**, e.g., a tracheary element loses its protoplasm and develops strong lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water.
2. Without differentiation, tissues such as xylem, epidermis or root cap would not form.
3. Since development is the sum of growth and differentiation, the plant could not develop roots, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
groundedIn: §13.2; §13.3; §13.4.2 — differentiation leads to maturation for specific functions; tracheary element example; root-cap and epidermis; development as sum of growth and differentiation; callus as a mass of undifferentiated cells

context: What would be expected to happen if:
stem: a rotten fruit gets mixed with unripe fruits
solution:
The unripe fruits would **ripen quickly**.

1. **Ethylene** is synthesised in large amounts by tissues undergoing **senescence** and by ripening fruits, so the rotten fruit releases ethylene.
2. Ethylene is a **gaseous** PGR and is highly effective in **fruit ripening**; it reaches the nearby unripe fruits and enhances their respiration rate during ripening.
3. In the same way, H.H. Cousins (1910) found that a volatile substance released from ripened oranges, later identified as ethylene, hastened the ripening of stored unripened bananas.
groundedIn: §13.4.3.4; §13.4.2 — ethylene synthesised in large amounts by senescing tissues and ripening fruits; gaseous; highly effective in fruit ripening; Cousins' oranges hastened ripening of stored bananas

context: What would be expected to happen if:
stem: you forget to add cytokinin to the culture medium.
solution:
The cultured cells would **not divide** to form a proliferating **callus**, and shoot formation would not be promoted.

1. Cytokinins have specific effects on **cytokinesis** (cell division). F. Skoog and co-workers found that callus from internodal segments of tobacco stems proliferated **only if**, in addition to auxins, the medium was supplemented with a cytokinin source (extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk or DNA).
2. Cytokinins also help to produce new leaves and promote **adventitious shoot formation**, so without them the culture would fail to form shoots.
groundedIn: §13.4.2; §13.4.3.3 — Skoog: callus proliferated only if, in addition to auxins, the medium had vascular tissue extract, yeast extract, coconut milk or DNA; kinetin as the cytokinesis-promoting substance; cytokinins produce new leaves and adventitious shoots
